title.en: Motown, Stax, the Invasion, and America’s reply
title.zh: Motown，Stax，英伦入侵和美国的回应

summary.en: The British Invasion hits white pop hard; Black pop led by Motown and Stax largely rides through and keeps thriving.
summary.zh: 英伦入侵一定程度上打击了白人流行乐，但是以Motown和Stax为代表的黑人流行乐却鲜有受其影响，仍旧欣欣向荣。

body.zh:
英伦入侵一定程度上打击了白人流行乐，但是以Motown和Stax为代表的黑人流行乐却鲜有受其影响，仍旧欣欣向荣。

我们稍微暂停一下，整理一下这三章以来讨论过的风格。因为在60年代中期，它们的发展从各方面来说都是平行的。我们从64年到66、67年的英伦入侵开始讲，从《I Want to Hold Your Hand》一直讲到67年发行的《Sgt. Pepper》。对此，美国乐坛对英伦入侵的回应，经过了最初许多白人流行乐手感到被击败，被英国乐手淘汰出局，到65年夏天美国音乐的回归，涌现出了上章讨论过的像Bob Dylan、The Byrds等一系列民谣摇滚艺人。而我们这章说的Motown厂牌，其功成名就与英伦入侵是平行的，甚至在英伦入侵之前就有畅销金曲，并在英伦入侵的时期里持续升温，似乎没有受到其影响。而Stax厂牌的崛起，则略微在英伦入侵之后，我们讲到了65、66年，又讲了67、68年的Aretha Franklin这种南方灵魂乐风格。那么当时的影响究竟是怎样的呢？
要我说，由于Motown的存在，黑人流行乐在整个60年代持续占据着流行乐榜单。从The Shirelles、The Ronettes、The Crystals、Ben E. King、The Drifters，再到The Supremes、The Temptations、Four Tops 以及 Martha and the Vandellas。这一路看过来，虽然大本营似乎从纽约转移到了底特律，但这些黑人流行音乐人始终相对稳定地占领着榜单前几名。
Stax于60年代下半叶在流行音乐圈的崛起，或多或少地拓宽了黑人流行乐的市场，因为他们的音乐真正地毫不避讳地融入了许多黑人元素，特别汲取了福音音乐传统。当我们提到Stax，其实谈论的是南方灵魂乐这一音乐风格，因为我们所谈到的很多音乐并不是Stax录制的，甚至不是在孟菲斯录制的。重点是在这段时间，很多新兴的音乐及其制作人、歌曲创作者的角色定位，依然受到老派音乐商业模式的制约，尤其是在黑人流行乐中。还有一个我反复强调的重点，黑人流行乐并没有被英伦入侵挤下排行榜。英伦入侵之所以重要，是因为它是给流行音乐注入强心剂的生力军，但它并没有阻断别人的生路。它的确带来了改变，但它没有把黑人音乐挤下榜单。Motown跟Stax对英伦入侵的反应远没有白人流行音乐来得强烈。从各方面来看，虽然不是完全没有影响，但比起白人流行乐队诸如Paul Revere & the Raiders、The Byrds那种想要拿出点什么来回应The Beatles的心情，黑人流行乐相对来说受到的影响小得多。
真正引起我注意的是Motown与Stax的相似性，因为就像我多次提及的，他们总是被放在对立的位置，总是在探讨到底谁的音乐更“黑人”。但我们来看看他们的相似性，两个厂牌都有录制旗下音乐的专属录音棚，特别是Stax录音棚，就算是 Muscle Shoals Sound录音室这个Stax方的外援，它依然是个专为歌曲创作者跟乐队服务的独立录音棚。这两家厂牌相似之处非常多，那么Stax真的比Motown更“黑人”吗？当我们讨论这些种族相关的问题时，需要谨慎一些。
我们来做个简单的比较吧。Motown的乐手与艺术家们几乎全是黑人，虽然Motown中有几个白人吉他手，有些白人参与Motown运营，但它还是个由黑人所有的厂牌，几乎都是黑人。Stax由白人拥有，而值得赞赏的是，黑人白人的数量基本上是对半开。所以某方面来说，如果纯粹数人头论输赢，Motown是个更“黑人”的厂牌。但是不得不说，事情往往没有这么简单，尤其是涉及种族问题的时候。我们还是来看看，围绕这个主题的其他佐证材料吧。
Stax的唱片确实听起来比较无拘无束，在许多Stax发行的南方灵乐唱片中，有许多绝不会在Motown的唱片中出现的元素，人声的部分尤甚。若改由Berry Gordy操刀，他大概会减少一些其中出现的许多即兴的、受到福音音乐影响的痕迹，因为他怕这些元素会使一些白人听众敬而远之。所以Motown的音乐，人为限制与制作的痕迹很重。讽刺的是，这很像50年代Atlantic Records在与Chess Records等厂牌分庭抗礼时的制作手法。当然，这次Motown是那个精心雕琢的唱片公司，Stax虽与Atlantic相关，却是较无拘无束的那个，Motown明显更以流行为导向，更加跨界到主流。
（小鼓注：关于Atlantic与Chess的故事，可参见第1章第8节，《前夜 8 – 1945年后的R&B》。Atlantic的出品较精致，而Chess的出品较粗犷，此恰似Motown与Stax的区别。之所以说Stax与Atlantic有关系，首先是因为两家厂牌之间有授权分销的业务关系，其次Atlantic旗下的录音师Tom Dowd也曾为Stax的录音棚服务；这些内容可参见本章第4节，《美国灵魂乐镇和南部灵魂乐》。所谓讽刺则是指，Atlantic本是注重精致的厂牌，与Atlantic紧密合作、乃至于共用一个录音师的Stax却宣扬粗犷。综上所述，Covach教授可能试图说明，Motown之精和Stax之粗在相当程度上都是商业考虑的产物。如果秉持严谨的学术态度，就不宜简单地将Motown与Stax的出品差异归结为文化自觉层面的强烈对抗。）
因此当我们在比较Stax与Motown时，这些都是需要考虑的因素。请想想，你是觉得Stax比Motown更“黑人”、更真实而且接受自己的黑人身份，还是说你认为“Motown违背了黑人精神”这个评价本身是有失公允的。这是个开放性问题，我把这个问题留给你们。接下来，我们将要着重讲讲一个人，无论在哪一方面，他都不落人话柄地秉持黑人精神，他就是灵魂乐教父——James Brown。
body.en:
The British Invasion hits white pop hard; Black pop led by Motown and Stax largely rides through and keeps thriving.

Pause and sort the styles of these three chapters. In the mid-1960s they run, in many ways, in parallel. We begin with the British Invasion from 1964 through 1966–67—“I Want to Hold Your Hand” through 1967’s Sgt. Pepper. America’s reply runs from many white pop players feeling beaten, edged out by British acts, to a summer-1965 return—folk-rock figures like Dylan and the Byrds from last chapter. Motown’s rise runs parallel to the Invasion, with hits even before it, and keeps heating through Invasion years as if barely touched. Stax rises a bit after the Invasion—we covered 1965–66, then 1967–68 Aretha and that southern-soul style. So what are the effects?
I would say: because of Motown, Black pop holds the pop charts through the 1960s. From the Shirelles, Ronettes, Crystals, Ben E. King, Drifters to the Supremes, Temptations, Four Tops, Martha and the Vandellas—looking along that line, the base seems to shift from New York to Detroit, but Black pop artists keep a relatively steady grip on the top slots.
Stax’s late-1960s rise in the pop world more or less widens Black pop’s market, because the music openly folds in Black elements, especially gospel tradition. When we say Stax we often mean southern soul as a style—much of what we discussed is not cut at Stax, or even in Memphis. The point is that in this stretch many new sounds and the roles of producers and writers still sit inside older music-business patterns, especially in Black pop. Another point I keep stressing: Black pop is not pushed off the charts by the Invasion. The Invasion matters as a fresh force injecting energy into pop, but it does not cut others’ livelihood. It changes things; it does not shove Black music off the lists. Motown and Stax react to the Invasion far less intensely than white pop. Influence is not zero, but compared with white pop bands like Paul Revere & the Raiders or the Byrds wanting something to answer the Beatles with, Black pop is affected much less.
What catches my eye is Motown–Stax similarity—because, as I keep saying, they are always set in opposition: whose music is “Blacker.” Look at likenesses: both labels have dedicated studios for their music; even Muscle Shoals Sound as a Stax-side ally remains an independent room serving writers and bands. Similarities are many. Is Stax really “Blacker” than Motown? On race questions we need care.
A simple comparison. Motown’s players and artists are almost all Black; a few white guitarists and some white staff in operations, but it is Black-owned and almost entirely Black. Stax is white-owned; to its credit, Black and white numbers are roughly half and half. Pure head-count, Motown is the “Blacker” label. But things are rarely that simple, especially with race. Look at other evidence around the theme.
Stax records do sound freer. Many southern-soul sides on Stax carry elements that would rarely appear on Motown—especially vocals. In Gordy’s hands he would likely trim much of the improvisation and gospel-tinged traces, fearing they would push some white listeners away. So Motown’s music shows heavy human constraint and production. Ironically, that resembles how 1950s Atlantic worked against Chess and similar labels. This time Motown is the carefully crafted company; Stax, though tied to Atlantic, is the freer one; Motown is clearly more pop-oriented, more crossover to the mainstream.
(Translator’s note / 小鼓注: For the Atlantic–Chess story, see Chapter 1, Section 8, “Prelude 8 – R&B after 1945.” Atlantic’s output is more polished; Chess’s is rougher—rather like Motown versus Stax. Stax relates to Atlantic first through licensing/distribution, and second because Atlantic engineer Tom Dowd also works Stax’s studio; see this chapter’s Section 4, “Soulsville U.S.A.: Stax and southern soul.” The irony is that Atlantic is the polish-minded label, yet Stax—closely partnered with Atlantic and even sharing an engineer—sells a rougher sound. In sum, Professor Covach may be saying that Motown’s polish and Stax’s roughness are to a considerable degree products of commercial calculation. A careful scholarly stance should not reduce Motown–Stax sonic differences to a simple culture-war of identity.)
So when we compare Stax and Motown, weigh these factors. Do you find Stax Blacker, more authentic, more accepting of Black identity—or do you find the charge that “Motown betrayed Black spirit” itself unfair? Open question; I leave it with you. Next we focus on one person who, on every count, holds Black spirit without inviting that charge: the Godfather of Soul—James Brown.
